system.one_liner: An attack on Chatbot Arena: an adversary identifies which model wrote a response and votes to push a target model up the leaderboard.

content.variant_note: cartoon users, an adversary and chatbot robots act out how votes are collected and how the leaderboard shifts, in three captioned scenes
content.argues: Chatbot Arena's anonymous pairwise voting can be gamed: an adversary who tells which model wrote a response can vote it up and shift the leaderboard ranking.
content.subject: A three-step cartoon of how Chatbot Arena collects votes and how an adversarial voter moves the leaderboard.

lessons.what_to_learn: Stage an attack as captioned cartoon scenes: thin grey lines for every possible link and thick colour lines for the ones used, one reserved colour (red) for the adversary on icon, label and text, and a before / after table at the end to show the damage.
lessons.suits: Threat-model or failure-mode illustrations of interactive platforms (leaderboards, marketplaces, annotation or feedback loops) where one actor's behaviour changes a ranking or a dataset.

evidence: Chatbot Arena compiles a model leaderboard using crowdsourced user votes and is therefore vulnerable to manipulation through adversarial voting.
genuine users vote based on quality, while adversarial users may exploit classifiers to break anonymity
the voting results are incorporated into the leaderboard and the model identities are revealed

summary: The paper shows that voting-based LLM leaderboards such as Chatbot Arena can be manipulated by adversarial votes. Figure 1 acts the attack out in three captioned scenes with cartoon characters. Step 1: five users and four coloured chatbot robots are tied to a central Chatbot Arena box, with thick blue curves marking the one user and the two randomly chosen models of this run. Step 2: two anonymous response cards are voted on by a normal user, who judges quality, and a devil-faced adversarial user, who uses a response model classifier to spot their own model. Step 3: before and after leaderboards show the targeted red robot rising from No.2 to No.1 while the teal robot falls.
summary_zh: 论文指出 Chatbot Arena 这类投票榜单可被恶意投票操纵。图 1 用三幕卡通场景讲述攻击：用户发起查询并随机抽两个模型，正常用户按质量投票，恶魔形象的攻击者借助分类器认出自己的模型，最后前后两张榜单显示目标模型从第二升到第一。
notes: Prior kinds worked-walkthrough / actor-interaction kept; side-by-side-contrast added for normal vs adversarial voter and the before / after leaderboards. The meaning of the thick blue curves (the path of this run) is read from the caption, which says two models are randomly selected. Icon counts are read off the picture (13 robots including the grey circled ones; the digest counts 25 placed bitmaps in all). The rank-change badges fit none of the marker kinds and are described in encoding instead. The robot hexes are approximate.
